question: Before reliable long-range radio aids existed, how were aircraft navigated across the oceans?

options.text: By following ground-based NDBs placed on ships along the route
By dead reckoning alone, with no means of fixing position at all
By VHF direction finding from coastal stations on both sides
By astro-navigation, taking sights on the sun, moon, stars and planets

explanation: Over the oceans there were no ground aids within range, so crews used the seafarer's method of celestial (astro) navigation. Long-range radio systems giving global cover only arrived around the 1970s, and today satellite systems have taken navigation back into space.

question: What is the accepted view on the future of ground-based radio aids now that satellite navigation (GNSS) is the standard?

options.text: All ground aids will be withdrawn once GNSS covers every airport
GNSS will be used only as a back-up to the ground-based aids
Some ground aids must be kept as a back-up to GNSS, en route and for approaches
Ground aids will be kept only for oceanic flight where GNSS is weakest

explanation: GNSS is now the primary means for many operations, but a single system failure or jamming event would leave no alternative. The policy is therefore to retain a network of terrestrial aids (such as DME and ILS) to back up GNSS both en route and on approach.

question: What made it possible for air traffic control to handle much higher traffic densities from the 1930s onwards?

options.text: The development of radar, allowing aircraft to be identified and monitored
The development of HF radio, which allowed position reports over the ocean
The introduction of NDBs on every airway intersection
The introduction of VHF voice frequencies for every sector

explanation: Radar lets a controller see and identify each aircraft, so separation can be reduced safely and more aircraft can use the same airspace. Where radar cannot be installed (oceans, remote land), satellite-based surveillance now provides a similar service.

question: A direct current (DC) flows steadily through a straight wire. What field forms around the wire?

options.text: An electric field radiating outwards as a radio wave
A magnetic field, perpendicular to the direction of current flow
A magnetic field, parallel to the direction of current flow
No field, because the current is not alternating

explanation: Any current produces a magnetic field around the conductor at right angles to the current. With steady DC that field is constant, so nothing is radiated — radiation needs a changing (alternating) current.

question: Why does an alternating current at a high frequency radiate energy from a wire, while one at a very low frequency hardly does?

options.text: At high frequency the electric and magnetic fields become parallel and add together
At low frequency the magnetic field is too strong to leave the wire
At high frequency the field cannot collapse before the next reversal, so energy leaves the wire
At high frequency the wire's resistance rises and the lost heat becomes radio energy

explanation: As the current reverses, the magnetic field must collapse and rebuild in the opposite sense. At low frequency it has time to return to zero; at high frequency the new field builds before the old one has gone, and energy is pushed out into space as an electromagnetic (radio) wave.

question: A radio wave is best described as:

options.text: An electric field that alternates in turn with a separate magnetic field
Electromagnetic energy with an electric field at right angles to a magnetic field
Electromagnetic energy with electric and magnetic fields lying in the same plane
A pressure wave carried by the molecules of the atmosphere

explanation: A radio wave is electromagnetic radiation, made of an electric (E) field and a magnetic (H) field that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. It needs no medium, unlike sound, which is a pressure wave in air.

question: Relative to the radiating wire (aerial), how are the two components of the radiated energy arranged?

options.text: The electric field is parallel to the wire; the magnetic field is perpendicular to it
Both fields are parallel to the wire and in phase with each other
Both fields are perpendicular to the wire and to each other
The magnetic field is parallel to the wire; the electric field is perpendicular to it

explanation: The E field lies in the same plane as the aerial, and the H field is at right angles to it. That is why the aerial's orientation sets the polarization, which is defined by the E field.

question: The polarization of a radio wave is defined by the plane of its:

options.text: Electric or magnetic field, whichever is the stronger

explanation: Polarization is the plane of the electric (E) field. Because the E field is parallel to the transmitting aerial, the plane of the aerial decides the polarization.

question: A transmitting aerial is mounted horizontally. What polarization will its signal have?

options.text: Circular polarization, rotating to the right
Polarization that changes with the frequency used

explanation: The electric field lies in the plane of the aerial, so a horizontal aerial produces a horizontally polarized wave and a vertical aerial a vertically polarized one.

question: For the strongest received signal, how should the receiving aerial be aligned with a linearly polarized wave?

options.text: In the same plane as the wave's polarization
Pointing along the direction from which the wave is arriving
At 45° to the wave's polarization, to receive both fields

explanation: Maximum signal is induced when the receiving aerial lies in the same plane as the incoming electric field. A vertically polarized wave therefore needs a vertical receiving aerial; an aerial at 90° would pick up very little.

question: Which type of aerial is one common way of producing circular polarization?

options.text: A loop aerial used for direction finding

explanation: Circular polarization can be produced in several ways; a helical (corkscrew) aerial is the classic one. A plain dipole or whip gives linear polarization.

question: In a circularly polarized wave, what does the electric field do?

options.text: It alternates between vertical and horizontal every half second
It stays fixed in the vertical plane while the magnetic field rotates
It rotates once for every wavelength of distance flown by the aircraft
It rotates, completing one turn per cycle of the wave

explanation: The electric field (and so the magnetic field) rotates at the wave's own frequency, either right-handed or left-handed depending on how the aerial array is arranged.

question: Why does circular polarization help a radar to reject returns from rain?

options.text: Raindrops absorb circularly polarized energy completely, so they give no echo
Reflection from round water droplets reverses the rotation, so the receiver can reject it
Rain returns arrive with vertical polarization and are filtered out
Circular polarization uses a lower frequency that rain does not reflect

explanation: When a circularly polarized pulse reflects off near-spherical droplets, the sense of rotation is reversed. An aerial set up for the original sense largely rejects the reversed echo, so precipitation clutter is reduced while echoes from irregular targets remain.

question: Why is circular polarization an advantage for mobile users such as satellite navigation receivers?

options.text: It travels further through the ionosphere than linear polarization
It needs no aerial at all, only a tuned receiver
A simple dipole can receive it without careful alignment of the aerial
It cannot be affected by reflections from buildings or terrain

explanation: With linear polarization the receiving aerial must be aligned with the wave. A circularly polarized wave can be received by an aerial of the same orientation or a simple dipole in almost any attitude, which suits phones, aircraft and satellite receivers that move and turn.

question: What decides whether circular polarization rotates right-handed or left-handed?

options.text: The orientation of the aerial array

explanation: The sense of rotation is fixed by how the transmitting aerial array is arranged. A receiving aerial of the same orientation (or a simple dipole) will receive it.

question: The period (τ) of a radio wave is:

options.text: The distance travelled during one cycle
The time taken for the wave to reach the receiver
The number of cycles completed in one second
The time taken to complete one cycle

explanation: The period is a time — the duration of one cycle — normally measured in microseconds (1 µs = 10⁻⁶ s). The number of cycles per second is the frequency, and the distance in one cycle is the wavelength.

question: How are frequency (f) and period (τ) related?
explanation: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, so it is the reciprocal of the time for one cycle. Halving the period doubles the frequency.

question: A radio wave has a period of 0.25 µs. What is its frequency?
explanation: f = 1/τ = 1 / (0.25 × 10⁻⁶ s) = 4 000 000 Hz = 4 MHz. The distractors come from slipping a power of ten in the microsecond conversion.

question: A signal has a frequency of 2 MHz. What is its period?
explanation: τ = 1/f = 1 / (2 × 10⁶ Hz) = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ s = 0.5 µs. Higher frequency means a shorter period.

question: One megahertz (MHz) is equal to:
A frequency of 0.35 GHz is the same as:
explanation: 1 GHz = 1 000 MHz, so 0.35 GHz = 350 MHz. Converting units correctly matters before using the wavelength formulas.

question: At approximately what speed do radio waves travel?
explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation, like light, so they travel at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300 000 km per second).

question: Expressed in nautical miles, the speed of radio waves is about:
explanation: 300 000 km/s divided by 1.852 km per NM gives about 162 000 NM/s. This figure is used in radar and DME timing (about 12.36 µs per NM of radar range).

question: Wavelength (λ) is:

options.text: The height of the wave from the zero line to its peak
The distance a wave travels during one cycle
The distance from the transmitter to the first null
The time a wave takes to complete one cycle

explanation: Wavelength is a distance. Since the wave moves at speed c, in one period it covers λ = c × τ.

question: Which formula gives the wavelength from the frequency?
explanation: λ = c × τ and τ = 1/f, so λ = c/f. Wavelength and frequency are inversely proportional: double the frequency and the wavelength halves.

question: Using the short-cut λ (m) = 300 / f, in what unit must the frequency be entered?
explanation: 300 is 3 × 10⁸ m/s divided by 10⁶, so the formula works only with f in MHz and gives λ in metres. Similarly f (MHz) = 300 / λ needs λ in metres.

question: What is the wavelength of a VHF signal on 150 MHz?
explanation: λ = 300 / 150 = 2 m. The other figures come from a misplaced decimal or from multiplying instead of dividing.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 600 m. What is its frequency?
explanation: f = 300 / 600 = 0.5 MHz = 500 kHz. A 600 m wavelength is typical of MF.

question: What is the wavelength of a 400 kHz NDB transmission?
explanation: Convert first: 400 kHz = 0.4 MHz. λ = 300 / 0.4 = 750 m. Forgetting to convert to MHz gives 0.75 m; dividing the wrong way gives 1 333 m.

question: A radar works on a wavelength of 3 cm. What is its frequency?
explanation: Convert to metres first: 3 cm = 0.03 m. f = 300 / 0.03 = 10 000 MHz = 10 GHz, in the SHF band.

question: A transmitter's period is 0.1 µs. What wavelength does it radiate?
If the frequency of a radio wave is doubled, its wavelength:
explanation: Speed is fixed, so λ = c/f: wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency. Doubling f halves λ.

question: Between what limits does the radio part of the electromagnetic spectrum lie?
explanation: The radio spectrum runs from 3 kHz to 300 GHz and is divided into eight bands, from VLF up to EHF.

question: How is each radio frequency band related to the band next to it?

options.text: Each band covers frequencies a hundred times those of the band below it
Each band has the same width in megahertz as its neighbour
Each band covers frequencies twice those of the band below it
Each band covers frequencies ten times those of the band below it

explanation: The band edges go 3–30–300–3000 in each unit, so each band is a factor of ten above the one below. That also makes each band's wavelengths ten times shorter.

question: What are the limits of the LF band?
explanation: LF (Low Frequency) is 30–300 kHz, wavelengths 10 km to 1 km. Below it is VLF (3–30 kHz), above it MF (300–3 000 kHz).

question: What are the limits of the MF band?
explanation: MF (Medium Frequency) is 300–3 000 kHz (0.3–3 MHz), wavelengths 1 000 m to 100 m.

question: What are the limits of the HF band?
explanation: HF (High Frequency) is 3–30 MHz, wavelengths 100 m to 10 m. It is used for long-range communication.

question: What are the limits of the VHF band?
explanation: VHF (Very High Frequency) is 30–300 MHz, wavelengths 10 m to 1 m. 108–137 MHz is only the aviation part of it (VOR, localizer, voice).

question: What are the limits of the UHF band?
explanation: UHF (Ultra High Frequency) is 300–3 000 MHz, wavelengths 100 cm to 10 cm. 960–1 215 MHz is only the DME part of it.

question: What are the limits of the SHF band?
explanation: SHF (Super High Frequency) is 3–30 GHz, wavelengths 10 cm to 1 cm. Radio altimeters, weather radar and MLS work here.

question: Which two radio frequency bands have no civil aeronautical use?
explanation: VLF (3–30 kHz) and EHF (30–300 GHz) are not used for civil aviation navigation or communication. LF/MF carry NDBs, HF long-range voice and SHF the radars.

question: In which band(s) do NDBs operate?
explanation: NDBs and the aircraft ADF use LF and MF frequencies (roughly 190–1 750 kHz). MF is also used for some long-range communication.

question: Which aid uses the VHF band?
explanation: VOR, the ILS localizer, marker beacons, VDF and short-range voice all use VHF. DME and the glide path are UHF; weather radar is SHF.

question: Which group of systems all work in the UHF band?

options.text: ILS glide path, DME and SSR
Radio altimeter, weather radar and MLS
ILS localizer, VOR and marker beacons

explanation: UHF (300–3 000 MHz) carries the glide path, DME, SSR, satellite communication, GNSS and long-range radar. The localizer group is VHF; the radio altimeter group is SHF.

question: Which group of systems all work in the SHF band?

options.text: Radio altimeter, airborne weather radar and MLS
NDB, long-range HF and marker beacons

explanation: SHF (3–30 GHz) is used by the radio altimeter, airborne weather radar, MLS and short-range radars such as aerodrome surface movement radar.

question: Which band does long-range HF voice communication use?
explanation: Long-range communication uses HF (and some MF), because those frequencies can be refracted back to earth by the ionosphere. VHF is line of sight only.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 2.5 m. In which band does it lie?
explanation: f = 300 / 2.5 = 120 MHz, which is within 30–300 MHz. Wavelengths of 10 m to 1 m are always VHF.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 25 cm. In which band does it lie?
explanation: 25 cm = 0.25 m, so f = 300 / 0.25 = 1 200 MHz, inside 300–3 000 MHz. Wavelengths from 1 m down to 10 cm are UHF.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 2 000 m. In which band does it lie?
explanation: f = 300 / 2 000 = 0.15 MHz = 150 kHz, inside 30–300 kHz. Wavelengths from 10 km to 1 km are LF.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 50 m. In which band does it lie?
explanation: f = 300 / 50 = 6 MHz, inside 3–30 MHz. Wavelengths from 100 m to 10 m are HF.

question: A signal has a wavelength of 4 cm. In which band does it lie?
explanation: 4 cm = 0.04 m, so f = 300 / 0.04 = 7 500 MHz = 7.5 GHz, inside 3–30 GHz. Wavelengths from 10 cm to 1 cm are SHF.

question: A signal has a frequency of 5 GHz. What is its wavelength?
explanation: Convert to MHz first: 5 GHz = 5 000 MHz. λ = 300 / 5 000 = 0.06 m = 6 cm, in the SHF band.

question: A signal has a frequency of 2 182 kHz. In which band does it lie?
explanation: 2 182 kHz = 2.182 MHz, which is inside 300–3 000 kHz (0.3–3 MHz): the MF band, even though it is close to HF.

question: A signal has a frequency of 329 MHz. What is its wavelength, and which band is it in?
explanation: λ = 300 / 329 ≈ 0.91 m = 91 cm. 329 MHz lies in UHF (300–3 000 MHz) — it is in fact an ILS glide path frequency.

question: What range of wavelengths belongs to the VHF band?
explanation: Frequency and wavelength run in opposite directions. VHF (30–300 MHz) covers 10 m down to 1 m; HF covers 100–10 m and UHF 1 m–10 cm.

question: What range of wavelengths belongs to the SHF band?
explanation: SHF (3–30 GHz) covers 10 cm down to 1 cm — "centimetric" wavelengths. EHF is 1 cm to 1 mm ("millimetric").

question: What condition must two signals meet before their phase can be compared?

options.text: They must start at the same phase
They must have the same amplitude
They must have the same frequency
They must have the same polarization

explanation: Phase comparison only has meaning between signals of the same frequency; with different frequencies the difference would change continuously. Amplitude does not matter.

question: In a phase comparison system, how are the two signals designated?

options.text: One is the reference signal, the other the variable signal
One is the master, the other the echo
One is the upper signal, the other the lower signal
One is the carrier, the other the sideband

explanation: One signal is the reference and the other the variable, and the measured difference is always expressed as the angle by which the variable lags the reference — a positive number from 0° to 360°.

question: How is the phase difference between a reference and a variable signal calculated?

options.text: The smaller of the two phase angles divided by the larger one
Variable phase minus reference phase, ignoring any minus sign
Reference phase plus variable phase, subtracting 360° if over 360°
Reference phase minus variable phase, adding 360° if the answer is negative

explanation: Phase difference = reference − variable. The answer must be positive, so a negative result has 360° added. This is the method used, for example, in a VOR receiver.

question: The reference signal is at 080° of phase when the variable signal is at 200°. What is the phase difference?
explanation: Reference − variable = 080° − 200° = −120°. A negative result has 360° added: −120° + 360° = 240°. Answering 120° is the common mistake of ignoring the sign.

question: The reference signal is at 300° of phase when the variable signal is at 045°. What is the phase difference?
explanation: Reference − variable = 300° − 045° = 255°, which is already positive, so no correction is needed.

question: On a graph, the reference wave travels through 90° from its own zero point before the variable wave reaches its zero point. What is the phase difference?
explanation: Start at zero phase on the reference wave and move in the positive direction until zero phase is reached on the variable wave. The angle the reference has moved through — here 90° — is the phase difference.
